name: Tyrannosaurus rex
dietDetails: Apex predator preying on large herbivores like Triceratops and Edmontosaurus.
discoveryHistory: First discovered by Arthur Lakes in Colorado (1874), later named and described by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1905.
interestingFacts: {"Had one of the strongest bite forces among all terrestrial animals, estimated at 35,000 to 57,000 Newtons.","Its tiny two-clawed arms were surprisingly strong, capable of lifting around 200 kilograms each.","Whether it had feathers is still debated, though direct fossil impressions show predominantly scaly skin."}
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 8,400 to 14,000 kg depending on study.
sources: [{"citation":"Osborn, H.F. (1905). Tyrannosaurus and other Cretaceous carnivorous dinosaurs. Bulletin of the AMNH 21(14): 259–265.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38613"}]

name: Triceratops horridus
dietDetails: Low-growing vegetation like ferns, cycads, and palms, cropped with its powerful beak.
discoveryHistory: First found near Denver, Colorado, in 1887 by George Lyman Cannon. Described by Othniel Charles Marsh.
interestingFacts: {"The large frill and three horns were likely used for defense against predators and in courtship or dominance displays.","Its skull was one of the largest of any land animal, reaching up to 2.5 meters in length.","Lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex, and fossil bones show healed T. rex bite marks, proving they clashed."}
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 6,000 to 12,000 kg depending on body mass calculations.
sources: [{"citation":"Marsh, O.C. (1889). Notice of new American dinosaurs. American Journal of Science 37(220): 331–336.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38861"}]

name: Velociraptor mongoliensis
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Peter Kaisen in 1923 at Flaming Cliffs.
interestingFacts: ["Retractable 9 cm sickle claw on second toe.", "Quill knobs on ulna proving presence of feathers.", "Slender upturned snout."]
sources: [{"citation": "Osborn, H.F. (1924). Amer. Mus. Novit.", "url": "https://hdl.handle.net/2246/3221"}]

name: Parasaurolophus walkeri
dietDetails: High and low vegetation, conifers, leaves, and twigs, processed with grinding dental batteries.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Alberta, Canada, in 1920 by William Parks. Described in 1922.
interestingFacts: {"The hollow, curved crest on its head functioned as a resonating chamber to produce low-frequency vocalizations.","Could walk on both two legs (when running or browsing) and four legs (when slow walking or grazing).","Its crest was also likely used for visual display and species identification."}
sizeNotes: Grew to about 9.5 meters long; weight estimated at 2.5 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Parks, W.A. (1922). Parasaurolophus walkeri, a new genus and species of crested trachodont dinosaur. University of Toronto Studies, Geological Series 13: 1–32.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38776"}]

name: Ankylosaurus magniventris
nameMeaning: Fused lizard with a great belly
dietDetails: Low-growing plants, ferns, and shrubs, cropped with its broad beak.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana by Barnum Brown in 1906. Described in 1908.
interestingFacts: {"Had a heavy armor of bony osteoderms and a massive bony club at the end of its tail, used for self-defense.","The tail club was supported by fused vertebrae, allowing it to deliver bone-shattering blows to attackers.","Lived in the same environments as Tyrannosaurus rex, serving as one of its most heavily fortified prey."}
sizeNotes: Ranged from 6 to 8 meters long; weighed roughly 5 to 8 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Brown, B. (1908). The Ankylosauridae, a new family of armored dinosaurs from the Upper Cretaceous. Bulletin of the AMNH 24(12): 187–201.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38827"}]

name: Carnotaurus sastrei
dietDetails: Medium-sized herbivores and small dinosaurs in open dry landscapes.
discoveryHistory: Found in Chubut Province, Argentina, by Anselmo Sastre in 1984 during an expedition led by José Bonaparte.
interestingFacts: {"Possessed two distinct, thick horns above its eyes, unique among carnivorous dinosaurs.","Its forelimbs were vestigial, even smaller than those of T. rex, and lacked claws entirely.","Had extremely fast leg muscles, making it one of the fastest running large theropods known."}
sizeNotes: Ranged from 7.5 to 9 meters in length; weight is estimated around 1.35 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Bonaparte, J.F. (1985). A horned Cretaceous carnosaur from Patagonia, Carnotaurus sastrei n.g. et n.sp. OS Museum Novitates: 1–16.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38602"}]

name: Quetzalcoatlus northropi
nameMeaning: Named after the Aztec feathered serpent god Quetzalcoatl
dietDetails: Small vertebrates, carrion, and terrestrial prey.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Big Bend National Park, Texas, by Douglas A. Lawson in 1971. Described in 1975.
interestingFacts: {"The largest known flying animal in Earth's history, with a wingspan comparable to a small private airplane.","When standing on the ground, it was as tall as a modern giraffe (around 5.5 meters).","Likely hunted on land by stalking prey on all fours, similar to modern marabou storks."}
sizeNotes: Wingspan: 10 to 11 meters; weight estimates range from 70 to 250 kg due to light, air-filled bones.
sources: [{"citation":"Lawson, D.A. (1975). Pterosaur from the Latest Cretaceous of West Texas: Discovery of the Largest Flying Creature. Science 187(4180): 947–948.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38507"}]

name: Pteranodon longiceps
dietDetails: Fishes, squids, and small marine organisms caught by diving.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1870 in the Smoky Hill Chalk of Kansas. It was the first pterosaur found outside Europe.
interestingFacts: {"Unlike earlier pterosaurs, it lacked teeth and had a bird-like beak.","Males had a large, backward-pointing crest on their skull, likely used for display and steering.","Fossils suggest they spent most of their time gliding over the Western Interior Seaway."}
sizeNotes: Wingspan: 5.6 meters for females, up to 7.2 meters for males. Weight: ~30 to 90 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Marsh, O.C. (1876). Notice of new Odontornithes and Pterosauria. American Journal of Science 11(66): 507–509.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38499"}]

name: Mosasaurus hoffmannii
dietDetails: Fish, ammonites, sharks, plesiosaurs, sea turtles, and even smaller mosasaurs.
discoveryHistory: First found in a chalk quarry near Maastricht, Netherlands, in 1764. The skull became famous when French revolutionary forces confiscated it in 1794.
interestingFacts: {"Not a dinosaur, but a giant marine reptile closely related to modern monitor lizards and snakes.","Had a second row of teeth (pterygoid teeth) on the roof of its mouth, preventing prey from escaping down its throat.","Propelled itself through water with a powerful, shark-like tail fin, using its flippers only for steering."}
sizeNotes: Large specimens reached up to 15 to 17 meters in length; weight is estimated at 10 to 15 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Mantell, G.A. (1829). A tabular view of the osseous remains of reptiles in the South-East of England. Transactions of the Geological Society of London 2(3): 421–424.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=36399"}]

name: Elasmosaurus platyurus
nameMeaning: Thin-plate lizard with a flat tail
dietDetails: Small bony fish, squids, and shelled cephalopods.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Kansas in 1867 by Theophilus Turner. Described by Edward Drinker Cope, who notoriously reconstructed the fossil with the head on the tail end.
interestingFacts: {"Had an extremely long neck consisting of 72 neck vertebrae, more than any other known animal.","Its neck was relatively rigid and could not be bent like a snake; it likely swam slowly beneath fish schools and darted its head up.","Swallowed small pebbles (gastroliths) to help grind food and control its buoyancy."}
sizeNotes: Total length was 10.3 meters (34 feet), of which 7.1 meters was the neck.
sources: [{"citation":"Cope, E.D. (1868). Remarks on a new enaliosaurian, Elasmosaurus platyurus. Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia 20: 92–93.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=36440"}]

name: Giganotosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1993 by Rubén Darío Carolini in Patagonia, Argentina.
• Formally named Giganotosaurus carolinii in 1995 by Coria and Salgado.
• Additional fragments of a potentially larger individual were found in later years.
interestingFacts: ["It had highly serrated teeth ideal for slicing flesh.","Possessed an elongated skull with an underdeveloped sense of smell compared to T. rex.","Likely preyed on giant titanosaur sauropods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Giganotosaurus carolinii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giganotosaurus"}]

name: Deinonychus
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1931 by Barnum Brown in Montana.
• John Ostrom redefined our understanding of dinosaurs by describing it in 1969.
• Ostrom's study of Deinonychus sparked the 'Dinosaur Renaissance'.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'terrible claw', referring to the large sickle claw on its foot.","Provided crucial evidence for the evolutionary link between dinosaurs and birds.","Often found in groups, suggesting possible pack-hunting behavior."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Deinonychus antirrhopus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinonychus"}]

name: Albertosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1884 by Joseph Burr Tyrrell in Alberta, Canada.
• Named Albertosaurus in 1905 by Henry Fairfield Osborn.
• A massive bonebed containing over 20 individuals was found in 1910.
interestingFacts: ["The bonebed discovery suggests it may have lived and hunted in packs.","Was lighter and faster than the closely related Tyrannosaurus rex.","Grew at a rapid pace, reaching mature size in less than 20 years."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Albertosaurus sarcophagus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albertosaurus"}]

name: Utahraptor
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1991 by a team led by James Kirkland in Utah.
• Officially named Utahraptor ostrommaysi in 1993.
• Additional specimens have since been found trapped in a potential quicksand predator trap.
interestingFacts: ["The largest known member of the dromaeosaurid family.","Its massive sickle claw could reach up to 9.4 inches in length.","Built for power rather than speed, unlike smaller raptors."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Utahraptor ostrommaysi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utahraptor"}]

name: Oviraptor
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1923 by George Olsen during an expedition to Mongolia.
• Named 'egg thief' because the first fossil was found atop a clutch of eggs.
• Later discoveries proved the eggs belonged to Oviraptor itself, and it was brooding them.
interestingFacts: ["Had a short, parrot-like beak with no teeth.","Likely possessed a crest on its head, similar to a modern cassowary.","Its brooding posture strongly resembles that of modern birds."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Oviraptor philoceratops description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oviraptor"}]

name: Majungasaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1896 by a French military officer in Madagascar.
• Originally named Megalosaurus crenatissimus by Charles Depéret in 1896.
• A complete skull discovered in 1996 clarified its classification as an abelisaurid.
interestingFacts: ["Provides the first unambiguous evidence of dinosaur cannibalism.","Had a distinctive dome on its skull, unique among theropods.","Possessed robust, muscular hind legs but very short arms."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Majungasaurus crenatissimus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majungasaurus"}]

name: Baryonyx
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1983 by amateur fossil hunter William Walker in Surrey, England.
• Described in 1986 by Alan Charig and Angela Milner.
• The holotype specimen included fish scales in its stomach region.
interestingFacts: ["Had a long, narrow snout resembling that of a crocodile.","Its large thumb claw was likely used to hook fish out of water.","Represents one of the earliest known spinosaurid dinosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Baryonyx walkeri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baryonyx"}]

name: Acrocanthosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the early 1940s in Oklahoma, USA.
• Named Acrocanthosaurus atokensis in 1950 by Stovall and Langston.
• A nearly complete skeleton 'Fran' was discovered in the 1990s.
interestingFacts: ["Characterized by tall neural spines along its back and neck.","Likely the apex predator of the Early Cretaceous in North America.","Its tracks have been found alongside those of giant sauropods in Texas."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Acrocanthosaurus atokensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acrocanthosaurus"}]

name: Dromaeosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1914 by Barnum Brown in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta.
• Named by Brown and Matthew in 1922.
• The type species of the family Dromaeosauridae.
interestingFacts: ["Had a heavily built skull with a stronger bite force than Velociraptor.","Relied on its jaws rather than its claws to kill prey.","Was one of the first 'raptor' dinosaurs discovered."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dromaeosaurus albertensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dromaeosaurus"}]

name: Troodon
discoveryHistory:
• A single tooth was discovered in 1856 by Ferdinand Vandeveer Hayden.
• Named by Joseph Leidy in 1856, making it one of the first dinosaurs named in North America.
• The genus has been considered a 'wastebasket taxon' due to confusing fossil fragments.
interestingFacts: ["Had one of the largest brain-to-body size ratios of any dinosaur.","Possessed large, forward-facing eyes, suggesting excellent nocturnal vision.","Its serrated teeth suggest an omnivorous diet."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Troodon formosus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troodon"}]

name: Gorgosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1913 by Charles M. Sternberg in Alberta, Canada.
• Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1914.
• Over 20 skeletons have been found, making it one of the best-represented tyrannosaurids.
interestingFacts: ["Coexisted with another tyrannosaurid, Daspletosaurus.","Had a lighter and more gracile build compared to T. rex.","Possessed a small horn-like crest in front of its eyes."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Gorgosaurus libratus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorgosaurus"}]

name: Daspletosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1921 by Charles Mortram Sternberg in Alberta.
• Dale Russell recognized it as a distinct genus and named it in 1970.
• Some specimens show bite marks from other tyrannosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["Was heavier and more robust than its contemporary, Gorgosaurus.","Considered by some scientists to be a direct ancestor of Tyrannosaurus rex.","Had proportionally larger teeth than T. rex."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Daspletosaurus torosus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daspletosaurus"}]

name: Styracosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• The first skull was collected in 1913 by Charles H. Sternberg in Alberta.
• Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
• Bonebeds suggest it lived in massive herds.
interestingFacts: ["Characterized by a spectacular frill adorned with up to six long spikes.","Its nose horn could grow up to two feet long.","Despite its fearsome appearance, it was a strict herbivore."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Styracosaurus albertensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styracosaurus"}]

name: Pachyrhinosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1946 by Charles M. Sternberg in Alberta, Canada.
• Described and named in 1950.
• The Pipestone Creek bonebed revealed hundreds of individuals.
interestingFacts: ["Lacked horns on its face, instead having massive bony bosses.","The bosses were likely used in head-butting combat.","Adapted to cold environments, with some fossils found near the Arctic Circle."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pachyrhinosaurus lakustai description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachyrhinosaurus"}]

name: Centrosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered by Lawrence Lambe in 1904 in Alberta, Canada.
• Lambe named the genus that same year based on incomplete remains.
• Enormous bonebeds in Dinosaur Provincial Park have yielded thousands of bones.
interestingFacts: ["Had a single large horn on its snout and small hornlets on its frill.","Lived in vast herds, potentially numbering in the thousands.","Many died in mass drowning events while crossing flooded rivers."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Centrosaurus apertus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrosaurus"}]

name: Chasmosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First remains found in 1898 by Lawrence Lambe.
• Formally named by Lambe in 1914.
• Multiple species have been identified from the Dinosaur Park Formation.
interestingFacts: ["Its frill had massive openings (fenestrae) to reduce weight.","The frill was likely brightly colored for display purposes.","Possessed small brow horns compared to later relatives like Triceratops."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Chasmosaurus belli description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasmosaurus"}]

name: Psittacosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1922 by the American Museum of Natural History expedition to Mongolia.
• Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1923.
• Hundreds of complete skeletons have been found, making it one of the most studied dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["Preserved fossils reveal it had long quill-like bristles on its tail.","We know its exact color pattern due to fossilized melanosomes.","It swallowed stones (gastroliths) to help grind up tough plant matter."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Psittacosaurus mongoliensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psittacosaurus"}]

name: Pentaceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1921 by Charles H. Sternberg in the San Juan Basin, New Mexico.
• Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1923.
• A massive skull was discovered in 1941, one of the largest of any terrestrial animal.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'five-horned face', including its two elongated cheek bones.","Has one of the largest skulls of any known land animal.","Lived further south than many of its northern ceratopsian relatives."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pentaceratops sternbergii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentaceratops"}]

name: Diabloceratops
discoveryHistory:
• The first skull was found in 2002 by Don DeBlieux in Utah's Wahweap Formation.
• Described and named by James Kirkland and colleagues in 2010.
• Represents one of the oldest known centrosaurine ceratopsids.
interestingFacts: ["Named for the pair of devil-like horns curving up from the back of its frill.","Had a shorter, deeper snout than most other ceratopsians.","Helped prove that early ceratopsids diversified in southern Laramidia."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Diabloceratops eatoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabloceratops"}]

name: Kosmoceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Found in 2006 by a volunteer in the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah.
• Formally named by Scott Sampson and colleagues in 2010.
• Its discovery shed light on dinosaur endemism in Late Cretaceous North America.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed 15 distinct horns or horn-like structures on its skull.","Its name translates to 'ornate horned face'.","The frill horns curled completely downward and forward."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Kosmoceratops richardsoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosmoceratops"}]

name: Zuniceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1996 by eight-year-old Christopher James Wolfe in New Mexico.
• Described and named by Douglas Wolfe and James Kirkland in 1998.
• Provides a crucial evolutionary link between earlier ceratopsians and later giants.
interestingFacts: ["The earliest known ceratopsian to feature true brow horns.","Lacked a solid frill, retaining a lighter, fenestrated structure.","Shows that large brow horns evolved before massive size in ceratopsians."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Zuniceratops christopheri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuniceratops"}]

name: Sinoceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2008 in the Shandong province of China.
• Described by paleontologist Xu Xing and colleagues in 2010.
• The first ceratopsid dinosaur ever found outside of North America.
interestingFacts: ["Features a frill adorned with forward-curving hornlets.","Lacked brow horns, but had a prominent nasal horn.","Its presence in Asia challenged prior theories of ceratopsid migration."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Sinoceratops zhuchengensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinoceratops"}]

name: Einiosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1985 by Jack Horner in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
• Named by Scott Sampson in 1995.
• Found in low-diversity bonebeds, indicating it lived in herds.
interestingFacts: ["Distinctive for a prominent nasal horn that curved forward like a bottle opener.","Its name means 'buffalo lizard' in the Blackfoot language.","Only adults possessed the heavily curved horn; juveniles had straight ones."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Einiosaurus procurvicornis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einiosaurus"}]

name: Achelousaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1987 by a team led by Jack Horner in Montana.
• Named by Scott Sampson in 1995 alongside Einiosaurus.
• Represents an evolutionary transition between Einiosaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["Had bony bosses on its snout and above its eyes instead of sharp horns.","Named after Achelous, a Greek river deity who had a horn torn off.","Fossils show a clear progression of horn loss within its lineage."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Achelousaurus horneri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achelousaurus"}]

name: Nasutoceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2006 in the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah.
• Described by Scott Sampson and colleagues in 2013.
• Added to the growing list of unique dinosaurs from the region.
interestingFacts: ["Featured an unusually short, thick snout.","Possessed curved brow horns that resembled those of modern cattle.","Its deep snout indicates it ate tough, fibrous vegetation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Nasutoceratops titusi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasutoceratops"}]

name: Edmontosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First remains were found in the late 19th century during the Bone Wars.
• Lawrence Lambe named the genus Edmontosaurus in 1917.
• Some of the best-preserved dinosaur mummies belong to this genus.
interestingFacts: ["Fossilized 'mummies' show detailed skin impressions and even a fleshy head comb.","Replaced its teeth continuously in a massive dental battery.","Was one of the main prey items for Tyrannosaurus rex."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Edmontosaurus annectens description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmontosaurus"}]

name: Corythosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1912 by Barnum Brown in Alberta, Canada.
• Named Corythosaurus by Brown in 1914.
• Early specimens featured extensive skin impressions.
interestingFacts: ["Its large, plate-like crest resembled a Corinthian helmet.","The crest was hollow and likely used for vocalization.","Lived alongside a vast diversity of other hadrosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Corythosaurus casuarius description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corythosaurus"}]

name: Maiasaura
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1978 by Marion Brandvold in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
• Jack Horner and Robert Makela named it Maiasaura in 1979.
• 'Egg Mountain' yielded nests, eggs, embryos, and juveniles.
interestingFacts: ["Provided the first solid evidence that dinosaurs cared for their young.","Hatchlings stayed in the nest and were fed by parents until they grew strong.","Lived in massive nesting colonies, much like modern seabirds."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Maiasaura peeblesorum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiasaura"}]

name: Tsintaosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1950 in Shandong Province, China.
• C.C. Young named the genus in 1958.
• Its distinctive crest was initially thought to be an artifact of preservation.
interestingFacts: ["Early reconstructions gave it a unicorn-like spike pointing directly up.","Recent studies show the crest was actually part of a larger, paddle-like structure.","Was one of the most prominent hadrosaurs in Late Cretaceous Asia."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Tsintaosaurus spinorhinus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsintaosaurus"}]

name: Lambeosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First materials collected in 1902 by Lawrence Lambe.
• William Parks named it Lambeosaurus in 1923 in honor of Lambe.
• Has had a complicated taxonomic history with many species consolidated over time.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed a bizarre crest shaped like a hatchet with a backward-pointing prong.","Its crest was hollow, serving as a resonating chamber.","Crest shape varied significantly based on age and sex."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Lambeosaurus lambei description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeosaurus"}]

name: Ouranosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1965 by French paleontologist Philippe Taquet in Niger.
• Formally described and named in 1976.
• Found in the same geological formation as Spinosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["Characterized by elongated neural spines forming a prominent sail on its back.","Its sail may have been used for thermoregulation or display.","Had a specialized thumb spike and a flattened, duck-like bill."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ouranosaurus nigeriensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouranosaurus"}]

name: Saurolophus
discoveryHistory:

name: Olorotitan

• Discovered in 1999 in the Amur Region of Far Eastern Russia.

name: Moros intrepidus
dietDetails: Fast-running cursorial carnivore hunting small vertebrates, mammals, and juvenile dinosaurs.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4d/Moros_intrepidus.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Moros intrepidus (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 4.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Moros_intrepidus.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Emery County, Utah, after a decade-long search led by Lindsay Zanno.
• Formally described in Communications Biology in February 2019.
• Represents the earliest diagnostic Cretaceous tyrannosauroid in North America.
interestingFacts: ["Filled the 70-million-year gap in North American tyrannosaur evolution.","Existed as a small, nimble predator when giant allosauroids (like Siats) were apex predators.","Extremely long leg bones indicate superior running speed and cursorial agility."]
sizeNotes: Small, lightweight cursorial tyrannosauroid standing less than a meter high at the hip.
sources: [{"citation":"Zanno, L. E. et al. (2019). Diminutive fleet-footed tyrannosauroid narrows the 70-million-year gap in the North American fossil record. Communications Biology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-019-0308-7"}]

name: Sauroposeidon proteles
nameMeaning: Lizard god of earthquakes, perfected before the end
dietDetails: High-canopy browser feeding on tall conifers, cycads, and ginkgos up to 18 meters above ground.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Gulf Coast / Interior Plains","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Antlers Formation, Cloverly Formation"}
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e6/Sauroposeidon_DB.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Sauroposeidon (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sauroposeidon_DB.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Four massive neck vertebrae discovered in Oklahoma in 1994 by prison trainer Bobby Cross.
• Initially stored as petrified wood for five years before paleontologists recognized their true nature.
• Formally described in 2000 by Mathew Wedel, Richard Cifelli, and Kent Sanders.
interestingFacts: ["Its neck reached up to 12 meters (39 feet) in length, accounting for over one-third of its total body length.","Cervical vertebrae were up to 1.4 meters long and filled with honeycombed internal air cells (trabecular bone).","Stood as tall as a 6-story building, allowing it to browse vegetation inaccessible to any other creature."]
sizeNotes: Stood up to 18 meters (60 feet) high, making it one of the tallest land animals to ever live.
sources: [{"citation":"Wedel, M. J. et al. (2000). Sauroposeidon proteles, a new sauropod from the Early Cretaceous of Oklahoma. Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1671/0272-4634(2000)020[0109:SPANSS]2.0.CO;2"}]

name: Vayuraptor agriculturalis
nameMeaning: Raptor of Vayu (Hindu god of wind)
dietDetails: Agile, swift carnivore preying on small ornithopods and lizard-like reptiles.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/23/Vayuraptor_agriculturalis.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Vayuraptor (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 4.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vayuraptor_agriculturalis.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2008 during agricultural field excavations in Chaiyaphum Province, Thailand.
• Formally described in 2019 by Adun Samathi and colleagues.
• Named in honor of the Sanskrit wind god Vayu due to its lightweight, fast-running skeletal adaptations.
interestingFacts: ["Coexisted with another medium-sized theropod, Siamraptor, in Early Cretaceous Thailand.","Ankle bones (astragalus and calcaneum) were fused together, enhancing biomechanical sprinting stability.","Species name 'agriculturalis' honors local farmers who assisted in uncovering the fossil site."]
sizeNotes: Medium-sized basal coelurosaurian theropod estimated at 4.5 meters in length.
sources: [{"citation":"Samathi, A. et al. (2019). Two new basal coelurosaurian theropods from the Early Cretaceous Sao Khua Formation of Thailand. Acta Palaeontologica Polonica.","url":"https://doi.org/10.4202/app.00624.2019"}]

name: Gillicus arcuatus
dietDetails: Filter-feeding teleost fish scooping up small fish and zooplankton in open sea waters.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Western Interior Seaway","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Smoky Hill Chalk"}
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9d/Gillicus_arcuatus.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Gillicus (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gillicus_arcuatus.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• First named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1872.
• Famous for the 'Fish-Within-A-Fish' fossil at the Sternberg Museum where a 4.3m Xiphactinus contains an intact 2m Gillicus in its ribcage.
• Abundant in Kansas chalk deposits.
interestingFacts: ["Best known as the swallowed prey in the famous 14-foot Xiphactinus specimen at Hays, Kansas.","Possessed numerous fine, needle-like gill rakers used to strain small marine organisms from sea water.","Had deeply embedded, thin circular scales that reduced turbulence during swift schooling swims."]
sizeNotes: Slender, 2-meter long ichthyodectid fish with fine, toothless or tiny-toothed jaws.
sources: [{"citation":"Bardack, D. (1965). Anatomy and evolution of chirocentrid fishes. University of Kansas Paleontological Contributions.","url":"https://hdl.handle.net/1808/3814"}]

name: Yutyrannus huali
dietDetails: Apex predator of cool, temperate Early Cretaceous forests, hunting sauropods and iguanodontians.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a2/Yutyrannus_huali.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Yutyrannus (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Yutyrannus_huali.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by local fossil collectors in Liaoning Province, China, and acquired by Xu Xing.
• Formally described in Nature in April 2012 by Xu Xing and colleagues.
• Three nearly complete skeletons of varying ages preserved extensive filamentous plumage.
interestingFacts: ["Holds the record as the largest direct feather-bearing animal in Earth's history (9 meters long, 1.4 tonnes).","Feathers were 20 cm long filamentous proto-feathers providing insulation in Liaoning's chilly 10°C climate.","Possessed a high median crest along its snout used for species display and intra-species communication."]
sizeNotes: Largest known dinosaur with direct, fossilized evidence of feathers.
sources: [{"citation":"Xu, X. et al. (2012). A gigantic feathered dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of China. Nature.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10906"}]

name: Nanotyrannus lancensis
dietDetails: Fast, highly active predator hunting agile prey such as ornithomimids, pachycephalosaurs, and young dinosaurs.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c5/Nanotyrannus_lancensis.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Nanotyrannus (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 4.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nanotyrannus_lancensis.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Skull discovered in 1942 by Charles W. Gilmore and initially named Gorgosaurus lancensis.
• Renamed Nanotyrannus by Robert Bakker, Michael Williams, and Philip Currie in 1988.
• Long debated whether it is a valid distinct genus or a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex; 2024 studies by Longrich & Saitta reignited support for its validity.
interestingFacts: ["Subject of one of the longest and most fiercely contested debates in paleontology history.","Had significantly more teeth (up to 36 in upper jaw) and larger forelimbs than adult T. rex.","Possessed extremely long, slender leg bones adapted for high-speed pursuit running."]
sizeNotes: Slender, long-limbed theropod measuring roughly 5 meters in length and weighing ~900 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Longrich, N. R., & Saitta, E. T. (2024). Taxonomic Status of Nanotyrannus lancensis: A Distinct Genus of Small Tyrannosaurid. Fossil Studies.","url":"https://doi.org/10.3390/fossils2010003"}]

name: Pyroraptor olympius
dietDetails: Agile, feathered pack hunter preying upon dwarf titanosaurs and iguanodontians on European islands.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e0/Pyroraptor_olympius.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Pyroraptor (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pyroraptor_olympius.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1992 following a forest fire at Mount Olympe near Trets, Provence, France.
• Formally described in 2000 by Ronan Allain and Philippe Taquet.
• Remains include distinctive sickle toe claws, teeth, limb bones, and vertebrae.
interestingFacts: ["Named 'Fire Thief' because its fossils were uncovered immediately after a major forest fire.","Possessed a curved 6.5 cm sickle claw on the second toe of each foot for gripping prey.","Fully covered in feathers with wing-like plumage along its forelimbs."]
sizeNotes: Small dromaeosaurid dinosaur measuring 1.6 meters long and standing knee-high.
sources: [{"citation":"Allain, R., & Taquet, P. (2000). A new dromaeosaurid (Dinosauria, Theropoda) from the Upper Cretaceous of Haute-Provence. Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1016/S1251-8050(00)00212-0"}]

name: Animantarx ramaljonesi
dietDetails: Low-level herbivore feeding on ferns, cycads, and low shrub vegetation.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e0/Animantarx_ramaljonesi.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Animantarx (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Animantarx_ramaljonesi.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1999 using radiological survey equipment by Ramal Jones.
• Formally described by Kenneth Carpenter, James Kirkland, Donald Burge, and John Bird in 1999.
• Discovered specifically due to radioactive signals emitted by fossilized bones.
interestingFacts: ["First dinosaur discovered exclusively via radiological radiation detection technology.","Possessed a heavily armored skull with small horn-like projections behind the eyes.","Lacked a tail club, relying instead on shoulder spikes and fused armor plates."]
sizeNotes: Small nodosaurid ankylosaur measuring approximately 3 meters.
sources: [{"citation":"Carpenter, K. et al. (1999). A new nodosaurid (Dinosauria: Ankylosauria) from the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah. Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1080/02724634.1999.10011140"}]

name: Segnosaurus galbinensis
dietDetails: Herbivorous theropod using long claws to hook branches and pluck leaves.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4b/Segnosaurus_galbinensis.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Segnosaurus (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Segnosaurus_galbinensis.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1973 in the Gobi Desert by Altangerel Perle.
• Formally described by Perle in 1979.
• Name-giver of the Segnosauria (now Therizinosauria) group.
interestingFacts: ["Bizarre theropod that evolved away from meat-eating to become a strict herbivore.","Possessed a massive pot belly to ferment tough plant vegetation.","Equipped with elongated, curved hand claws used to pull down tree branches."]
sizeNotes: Large therizinosaurid measuring 6 meters in length and weighing over 1 tonne.
sources: [{"citation":"Perle, A. (1979). Segnosauridae - a new family of theropods from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia. Transactions of the Joint Soviet-Mongolian Paleontological Expedition.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/checkTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38712"}]

name: Bajadasaurus pronuspinax
dietDetails: Low-level browser feeding on ferns, horsetails, and low vegetation using forward spines as defense.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/df/Bajadasaurus_pronuspinax.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Bajadasaurus (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 4.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bajadasaurus_pronuspinax.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2013 in Neuquén Province, Patagonia, Argentina.
• Formally described in Scientific Reports in 2019 by Pablo Gallina and colleagues.
• Preserved skull, neck vertebrae, and spectacular elongated neural spines.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed extremely long, thin neural spines along its neck that curved forward over its head.","The neck spines were likely covered in keratin sheaths, acting as defensive spikes against predators while grazing.","Eyes were positioned high on its skull, allowing it to look out for predators while lowering its snout to eat."]
sizeNotes: Dicraeosaurid sauropod measuring 9 meters long with dramatic forward-pointing neck spines.
sources: [{"citation":"Gallina, P. A. et al. (2019). A new long-spined dinosaur from Patagonia sheds light on sauropod defense mechanics. Scientific Reports.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-37943-3"}]

name: Fukuiraptor kitadaniensis
dietDetails: Medium-sized carnivore preying on ornithopods and sauropods in Early Cretaceous Japan.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6c/Fukuiraptor_kitadaniensis.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Fukuiraptor (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fukuiraptor_kitadaniensis.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1989 at the Kitadani Quarry in Katsuyama, Fukui Prefecture, Japan.
• Formally described in 2000 by Yoichi Azuma and Philip J. Currie.
• One of the most complete theropod skeletons found in Japan.
interestingFacts: ["Initially thought to be a dromaeosaurid due to a large hand claw, later recognized as a megaraptoran.","The state dinosaur mascot of Fukui Prefecture, Japan.","Possessed large hand claws used to grasp prey."]
sizeNotes: Medium-sized megaraptoran theropod reaching 4.2 meters in length.
sources: [{"citation":"Azuma, Y., & Currie, P. J. (2000). A new carcharodontosaurid theropod from the Lower Cretaceous of Japan. Cretaceous Research.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1006/cres.2000.0223"}]

name: Fukuisaurus tetoriensis
dietDetails: Herbivorous iguanodontian browsing on horsetails, ferns, and early flowering plants.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/eb/Fukuisaurus_tetoriensis.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Fukuisaurus (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fukuisaurus_tetoriensis.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1989 alongside Fukuiraptor in Katsuyama, Fukui, Japan.
• Described in 2003 by Yoichi Azuma and Pascal Godefroit.
• Preserved skull and jaw material showing unique kinetic chewing adaptations.
interestingFacts: ["Skull lacked the kinetic flexibility seen in advanced hadrosaurs, chewing with a rigid maxilla.","Coexisted with Fukuiraptor, Fukuititan, and Koshisaurus in Early Cretaceous Japan.","Equipped with a sharp beak for clipping tough vegetation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Kobayashi, Y. et al. (2003). A new iguanodontian dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous Kitadani Formation of Fukui, Japan. Memoir of the Fukui Prefectural Dinosaur Museum.","url":"https://www.dinosaur.pref.fukui.jp/archive/memoir/memoir002-126.pdf"}]

name: Suchomimus tenerensis
dietDetails: Semiaquatic predator snatching giant fish (Mawsonia) and young dinosaurs from Cretaceous rivers.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/36/Suchomimus_tenerensis.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Suchomimus (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Suchomimus_tenerensis.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1997 in the Ténéré Desert of Niger by team led by Paul Sereno.
• Formally described in Science in November 1998.
• Skeleton roughly 70% complete including skull, arms, claws, and vertebrae.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed a narrow 1.2-meter long crocodile-like skull lined with 100 conical teeth.","Had a massive 30 cm sickle claw on its thumb used to spear fish.","Featured a low neural spine sail reaching up to 60 cm high along its back."]
sizeNotes: Large spinosaurid theropod measuring 11 meters in length and weighing nearly 4 tonnes.
sources: [{"citation":"Sereno, P. C. et al. (1998). A long-snouted predatory dinosaur from Africa and the evolution of spinosaurids. Science.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1126/science.282.5392.1298"}]

name: Oxalaia quilombensis
dietDetails: Giant semiaquatic piscivore hunting giant lungfish and mawsoniid coelacanths in coastal mangrove swamps.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/eb/Oxalaia_quilombensis.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Oxalaia (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Oxalaia_quilombensis.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Premaxilla discovered in 1999 on Cajual Island, Maranhão, Brazil.
• Formally described in 2011 by Alexander Kellner and colleagues.
• Proved spinosaurines populated both South America and North Africa during the mid-Cretaceous.
interestingFacts: ["Named after Oxalá, the principal deity in the Afro-Brazilian Candomblé pantheon.","The largest carnivorous dinosaur recorded from Brazil.","Close relative of North African Spinosaurus, featuring double functional replacement teeth."]
sizeNotes: The largest theropod dinosaur discovered in Brazil, estimated between 12 to 14 meters long.
sources: [{"citation":"Kellner, A. W. A. et al. (2011). A new dinosaur (Theropoda, Spinosauridae) from the Cretaceous of Brazil. Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciências.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1590/S0001-37652011000100009"}]

name: Tropaeognathus mesembrinus
dietDetails: Ocean-going aerial piscivore skimming fish from the water surface using crested jaws.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/df/Tropaeognathus_mesembrinus.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Tropaeognathus (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tropaeognathus_mesembrinus.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Described in 1987 by Peter Wellnhofer from fossils in the Romualdo Formation, Brazil.
• 2013 skeleton specimen MN 6594-V described by Kellner et al. confirmed massive 8.2m wingspan.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest pre-azhdarchid flying reptiles known, with an 8.2-meter wingspan.","Possessed large convex keel-like crests on the tips of both upper and lower jaws.","Crests acted as rudders to stabilize jaws while dipping into water at high speed to catch fish."]
sizeNotes: Giant anhanguerid pterosaur with a wingspan reaching 8.2 meters (27 feet).
sources: [{"citation":"Kellner, A. W. A. et al. (2013). The largest pterosaur from Gondwana and other new anhanguerids from Brazil. Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciências.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1590/0001-37652013102912"}]

name: Coloborhynchus clavirostris
dietDetails: Coastal pelagic piscivore catching slippery marine fish with forward-pointing teeth.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/07/Coloborhynchus_clavirostris.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Life reconstruction of Coloborhynchus (Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Coloborhynchus_clavirostris.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Named by Richard Owen in 1874 based on a partial snout found in East Sussex, England.
• Re-evaluated by Rodrigues & Kellner in 2013, restricting the genus to European Valanginian strata.
interestingFacts: ["Featured a unique flattened front snout tip with teeth projecting forward at odd angles.","Equipped with a prominent crest along the front upper jaw.","Earliest recognized anhanguerid pterosaur in the European fossil record."]
sizeNotes: Pterosaur with an estimated wingspan of approximately 5 to 6 meters.
sources: [{"citation":"Rodrigues, T., & Kellner, A. W. A. (2013). Taxonomic review of the Ornithocheirus complex (Pterosauria). ZooKeys.","url":"https://doi.org/10.3897/zookeys.308.5559"}]
